title: Recruiter Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete recruiter resume example: sourcing, screening, pipeline management, and the exact bullet formula that turns hires made into proof hiring managers and applicant tracking systems both reward.
content_html:
Recruiter Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A recruiter resume has one job: prove you can fill roles, not just work near hiring. Hiring managers do not hire for task lists, tool inventories, or pleasant adjectives alone. They hire for roles filled, pipelines built, time-to-fill cut, and offers accepted: the requisition you owned, the action you took, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: A recruiter resume should include a summary naming the roles you hire for and your strongest hiring result, a skills section with sourcing, candidate screening, interview coordination, and offer management, experience bullets pairing each hiring duty with the hires made, the time saved, or the pipeline built, and proof of judgment through roles filled.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: requisition + action + result — the roles you filled, the pipeline you built, the time-to-fill you cut.
  • Lead with the roles you hire for and your headline hiring result: 120 roles filled in a year, time-to-fill cut from 45 days to 28, offer acceptance at 92%.
  • Spell tools exactly as postings do — LinkedIn Recruiter, Greenhouse, Lever, Workable — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show impact through counts, percentages, and ranges, never through confidential details: name the result, withhold the private detail.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a hiring manager what separates a keep-forever recruiter from a risky one and it won’t be “great with people.” It’ll be:

  • Roles that actually get filled. Requisitions closed on time, with hires who stay — not pipelines that look busy and close nothing.
  • Sourcing that finds people. Candidates found where others stop looking, and a talent pool that keeps producing instead of starting from zero every time.
  • Screening with judgment. Shortlists hiring managers trust, because the recruiter understood the role instead of matching keywords.
  • Process that respects everyone. Candidates kept informed, interviews coordinated without chaos, and offers closed without losing people to silence.
  • Stakeholders who stay aligned. Hiring managers briefed properly, expectations managed honestly, and difficult roles filled without drama.

Recruiter Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for a recruiter hiring technology roles. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: requisition, action, result.

FUNKE ALABI
Lagos · (234) 555-0147 · funke.alabi@email.com · linkedin.com/in/funkealabi

SUMMARY
Recruiter with 6 years hiring technology and operations roles, currently filling 120 roles a year across engineering, product, and support. Cut time-to-fill from 45 days to 28, hold offer acceptance at 92%, and built a talent pool of 3,000 pre-screened candidates. Known for shortlists hiring managers trust and candidates who stay informed.

SKILLS
Candidate sourcing · Screening · Interview coordination · Offer management · Talent pipelining · Stakeholder management · LinkedIn Recruiter · Greenhouse · Lever · Workable · Indeed · Boolean search · Salary benchmarking · Employer branding

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Senior Recruiter — Northgate Talent Partners, Lagos | 2021–Present

  • Own full-cycle hiring for 120 roles a year across engineering, product, and support: sourcing, screening, interview coordination, and offers, with time-to-fill cut from 45 days to 28.
  • Built a talent pool of 3,000 pre-screened candidates across 6 functions, so a third of new requisitions now start from warm candidates instead of cold outreach.
  • Hold offer acceptance at 92% by briefing candidates honestly on role, pay range, and timeline, and by closing offers within 48 hours of the final interview.
  • Run structured screening for 40 requisitions at a time, cutting hiring-manager interview time by a third with shortlists they actually hire from.
  • Partner with 12 hiring managers on intake briefs, resetting unrealistic requirements before sourcing starts and keeping requisitions realistic from day one.
  • Lead campus and referral drives that added 400 candidates to the pipeline in a year, including the hardest-to-fill senior engineering roles.

Recruiting Coordinator — Halcyon Staffing Group, Lagos | 2019–2021

  • Coordinated interviews for 25 open roles at a time — scheduling, candidate communication, and feedback collection — the work that led into a recruiter role.
  • Screened 200 applicants a month against role briefs, passing only candidates who matched the must-haves and cutting hiring-manager review time in half.
  • Kept every candidate informed within 48 hours of each stage, ending the silent rejections that had damaged the agency’s reputation.
  • Built the agency’s first sourcing tracker, so recruiters stopped re-contacting the same candidates and pipeline data stayed accurate.

EDUCATION
BSc, Psychology — 2019

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: roles hired, tenure, and headline proof in three lines

The example opens with the roles hired and tenure, then the proof: roles filled, time-to-fill cut, offer acceptance held. Without recruiter experience yet, lead with equivalent scope: “sourced and screened 200 applicants for 15 open roles, coordinating interviews for hiring managers across three teams.”

Skills: tools and duties exactly as postings spell them

Recruiting postings are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Name your tools (LinkedIn Recruiter, Greenhouse, Lever) and your duties (candidate sourcing, screening, interview coordination). “Great with people” is not a keyword; “candidate sourcing” is.

Experience: every bullet pairs a hiring duty with the result gained

The pattern is requisition + action + result: “cut time-to-fill from 45 days to 28 by building a pre-screened talent pool”; “hold offer acceptance at 92% by closing offers within 48 hours.” Scope matters too — roles filled, candidates screened, hiring managers supported, pipelines built.

Impact: show it through counts and percentages, never through secrets

Every recruiter claims impact; the strong ones prove it by naming the result and withholding the confidential detail: roles filled, time saved, offers accepted. One bullet about a pipeline built or a hard role filled proves the judgment hiring managers pay for, and separates a recruiter resume from a task list.

Recruiter Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Sourcing & screening: candidate sourcing, Boolean search, talent pipelining, screening, shortlisting, LinkedIn Recruiter, Indeed (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Process & coordination: interview coordination, offer management, stakeholder management, onboarding handover, Greenhouse, Lever, Workable.
  • Judgment & communication: salary benchmarking, employer branding, candidate experience, hiring-manager partnership, negotiation.
  • Tools: LinkedIn Recruiter, Greenhouse, Lever, Workable, Indeed, Google Workspace, Slack, Zoom.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Recruiter resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost Recruiter Interviews

  1. Task lists instead of hires. “Posted jobs and scheduled interviews” says nothing about the roles you filled. Every bullet needs a requisition, an action, and a result.
  2. Confidential details dressed as proof. Naming candidates, client companies, or offer figures to sound connected breaks the very trust the role requires. Use counts and percentages instead.
  3. Vague hiring language. “Managed recruitment” and “handled hiring” mean nothing to a hiring manager. Name the roles, the pipeline, and the result: roles filled, time-to-fill cut, offers accepted.
  4. Tools without matching bullets. A software list proves nothing on its own. Pair each tool with work that used it: the pipeline built, the roles filled, the candidates screened.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your sourcing section arrives as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a recruiter resume?

A summary naming the roles you hire for and your strongest hiring result; a skills section with sourcing, candidate screening, interview coordination, and offer management; experience bullets pairing each hiring duty with the hires made, the time saved, or the pipeline built; and proof of judgment through roles filled, not through vague claims of being a people person. Hires made beat hiring tasks listed alone.

Do I need a degree to become a recruiter?

Not always — recruiters come from sales, customer service, human resources, administration, and agency support roles, and many enter through a sourcing or recruiting-coordinator role plus a record of filling roles. Hiring managers weigh the roles you filled and the pipelines you built far more than a specific degree. A business or psychology degree helps for some employers, but a requisition filled, a time-to-fill cut, and an offer accepted prove more.

How do I show recruiting impact without revealing client or candidate details?

Use counts, percentages, and ranges instead of names: “filled 120 roles in a year” or “cut time-to-fill by a third” proves impact without naming a single client, candidate, or salary. Never name candidates, client companies, or offer figures that were not public. Recruiters read impact as judgment: the result stated plainly, the confidential detail withheld, and the scale implied by the roles themselves.

What is the difference between a recruiter and a human resources manager resume?

A human resources manager resume proves ownership of people operations: onboarding, performance, retention, and policy across a whole workforce. A recruiter resume proves ownership of hiring: sourcing, screening, pipelines, interviews, and offers for specific roles. The recruiter resume names the roles filled and the time-to-fill; the HR manager resume names the workforce managed and the programs built.

How do I write a recruiter resume with no recruiting title yet?

Lead with the closest equivalent work: the candidates you sourced, the interviews you coordinated, the hiring managers you supported, or the talent pools you built — then frame each as recruiting in miniature. “Sourced and screened 200 applicants for 15 open roles, coordinating interviews for hiring managers across three teams” proves the same skills at smaller scale. Add the tools recruiters use, run your resume through a free ATS grader first, and target recruiting coordinator or talent sourcer roles as stepping stones.

Should a recruiter resume list sourcing tools?

Yes — tool keywords are literal ATS filters in recruiting roles. List sourcing and hiring tools (LinkedIn Recruiter, Indeed, Greenhouse, Lever, Workable) exactly as postings spell them, and only tools you genuinely use. A tool without a matching bullet reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it: the pipeline built, the roles filled, the candidates screened.
